scenario: A new engineer starts Monday. It is the Friday before and nobody has confirmed their laptop or accounts.
question: What should the process have done?

options.text: Run a day-before readiness check by the process owner, escalate any gap immediately, and start preparation as soon as the offer is accepted.
Order equipment on the start date, since the new hire will be busy anyway.
Skip it. The new hire can sort accounts out with IT during the first week.

why: A poor first day is hard to recover from. Pre-boarding begins at offer acceptance, and the readiness check exists so gaps are caught while they can still be fixed.

scenario: IT is creating accounts for a new marketing hire. The quickest way is to copy a predecessor's access.
question: What is the right approach?

options.text: Use a role-based access template with minimum permissions, require justification and approval for extras, and review access at 30 and 90 days.
Copy the predecessor's access, then remove anything that seems wrong later.
Give broad access at first so the new hire never feels blocked.

why: A predecessor's access often includes outdated or excessive rights. Least privilege, an approval trail and scheduled reviews prevent avoidable security problems.

scenario: Several teams each do their part of onboarding. Tasks get missed and nobody sees the whole process.
question: What do you fix?

options.text: Name a single process owner accountable for the end-to-end experience, and assign every task to a role with an owner, due date and status on a shared checklist.
Add more email reminders for each team.
Make the hiring manager responsible for everything.

why: Clear ownership prevents tasks from falling between teams. A named process owner, often in HR or People Operations, also keeps the procedure current.

scenario: A manager wants to show a new hire sixty slides on day one so nothing is missed.
question: What works better?

options.text: Spread learning across the first weeks, with a welcome, working logins, a buddy, a small first task and an end-of-day check-in on day one.
Go ahead, then test the new hire with a quiz at the end of the week.
Skip day one and start with real work on day two.

why: Information overload helps no one. Day one should make the new hire feel welcome, able to log in and clear about what happens next.

scenario: Day 30 arrives. The manager is busy and suggests skipping check-ins because the new hire seems fine.
question: What should the 30-day check-in cover?

options.text: Review progress, address gaps, collect feedback on onboarding, confirm priorities and agree goals for the next 60 days, plus an access review.
Skip it. No news is good news.
A short chat about weekend plans, since formal reviews feel stiff.

why: The 30-60-90 structure makes goals, support and feedback explicit at each stage. New hires are also the best source of insight into what is broken in the process.
